 * prefetch — trusted-side lookahead scanner + parallel subresource pool (Hito 29).
 *
 * The confined worker requests subresources one at a time over a blocking pipe

 * latencies. This module brings the browser "preload scanner" pattern to the
 * TRUSTED side only: pf_scan (pure, no I/O) extracts <link rel=stylesheet href>
 * and <script src> references from the raw hostile HTML, and pf_pool_* downloads
 * a URL list in parallel through the SAME policy-gated fetch callback that would
 * serve the serial request. The worker protocol does not change; a pool miss just
 * falls back to the direct fetch. Removing the pool changes WHEN bytes are
 * fetched, never WHAT.
 *
 * Threads only touch the pool's own state (under its mutex) and the fetch
 * callback, which must be reentrant and apply the full network policy. take() and
 * finish() are called from the single orchestrating (load) thread.
 *
 * See spec/prefetch.md for the full contract.
 */

fbench -- turn the PNG pairs `make parity` leaves behind into something you can act on.  `make parity` prints one score per page. To fix a page you then need to SEE where the two engines part ways. This reads build/parity/<name>.fd.png (Freedom) and <name>.ff.png (Firefox) and, per page: * writes build/bench/<name>.sbs.png: Freedom | Firefox side by side, cropped to the band you ask for, so one Read shows the difference; * prints the first row where the pictures diverge and the worst 100 px bands by mean luminance difference, so you know which y to crop next; * ranks the pages by score and shows the delta against tests/parity/baseline.tsv.  Every page the README shows (README_PAGES) is also republished: its docs/img/compare-*.png is rewritten from the fresh pair and its score in the README table is updated, so the README always carries the latest render. --no-readme skips that.  Render time is measured too (spec/parity.md "Timing"): for the README pages -- or the pages named -- the REAL GUI window (tools/guitime.py: Xvfb + weston, same do_load/paint path as a user) and Firefox (tools/fftime.py: its own Performance Timeline) each report "navigation request -> painted and idle"; the medians are printed with the ratio and the delta against tests/parity/timing-baseline.tsv, saved to build/bench/timing.tsv, and written into the README between its fbench-timing markers. If the GUI cannot be run here (no Xvfb/weston) that is said and nothing is substituted. --no-time skips it.  Usage: fbench.py [--from Y] [--rows N] [--band PX] [--no-readme] [--no-time] [--time-runs N] [page ...]

def luma(img):
    return np.asarray(img.convert("L"), dtype=np.float32)

def bands(fd, ff, band):
    h = min(fd.shape[0], ff.shape[0])
    w = min(fd.shape[1], ff.shape[1])
    rows = np.abs(fd[:h, :w] - ff[:h, :w]).mean(axis=1)
    first = next((i for i, v in enumerate(rows) if v > 2.0), None)
    scored = []
    for y in range(0, h, band):
        scored.append((float(rows[y:y + band].mean()), y))
    scored.sort(reverse=True)
    return first, scored[:3]

def sbs(name, start, nrows):
    a = Image.open("%s/%s.fd.png" % (PARITY, name)).convert("RGB")
    b = Image.open("%s/%s.ff.png" % (PARITY, name)).convert("RGB")
    end = start + nrows
    a = a.crop((0, start, a.width, min(end, max(a.height, start + 1))))
    b = b.crop((0, start, b.width, min(end, max(b.height, start + 1))))
    h = max(a.height, b.height)
    canvas = Image.new("RGB", (a.width + b.width + 8, h + 16), (255, 0, 255))
    canvas.paste(a, (0, 16))
    canvas.paste(b, (a.width + 8, 16))
    d = ImageDraw.Draw(canvas)
    d.text((4, 2), "Freedom  y=%d" % start, fill=(255, 255, 255))
    d.text((a.width + 12, 2), "Firefox", fill=(255, 255, 255))
    os.makedirs(OUT, exist_ok=True)
    path = "%s/%s.sbs.png" % (OUT, name)
    canvas.save(path)
    return path

def publish_readme(name, score):
    """Rewrite the README picture of `name` and the score printed beside its label."""
    import re
    img, label = README_PAGES[name]
    path = sbs(name, 0, README_ROWS)
    os.makedirs("docs/img", exist_ok=True)
    Image.open(path).save("docs/img/" + img, optimize=True)
    if score == score:
        try:
            with open("README.md", encoding="utf8") as fh:
                text = fh.read()
            new = re.sub(r"(\b%s) \(\d+(?:\.\d+)?\)" % re.escape(label),
                         r"\1 (%.2f)" % score, text, count=1)
            if new != text:
                with open("README.md", "w", encoding="utf8") as fh:
                    fh.write(new)
        except OSError:
            pass

ffgeom -- Firefox geometry as TEXT, no image reading.  The `make geom` loop needs Firefox's getBoundingClientRect() numbers, and its only headless output here is a screenshot. This tool turns that screenshot into a text dump mechanically: the probe page replaces the body with a BIT-GRID canvas that encodes every measured rect as black/white cells, this script decodes the cells back into numbers, and prints one line per rect:  <index> <tag>.<class> top=<t> left=<l> w=<w> h=<h>  The encoding is a fixed grid, no OCR, no image model: - canvas 64px wide, each row 16 cells of 4x4px, one row per 16-bit VALUE - row 0: magic 0xC0DE (16 bits) + row count (16 bits) - then per rect: 4 rows (top, left, w, h), MSB first - rows continue per rect; the decoded count bounds the region read  The decoded values are what `make geom` prints beside Freedom's own --dump-layout, so a layout difference reads as two columns of numbers instead of being guessed from pixels. The canvas is white and fixed at the top-left of the viewport, so the grid region carries no underlying page ink.  Usage: ffgeom probe <page.html> <selector> <out.html> ffgeom decode <screenshot.png>  Both steps run through `make geom` (the Makefile is the single source of truth); this script is the thin worker it delegates to. Pure python, no dependencies, no network. It reads only local files the harness produced.

def _word_reader(path):
    """Loads a probe screenshot and returns a function reading 16-bit words from
    the bit-grid at (x0, y0). Shared by `decode` (rects) and `height` (the page's
    real scrollHeight)."""
    width, height, channels, rows = load_rows(path)
    if width < 64:
        raise ValueError("%s: narrower than the 64px grid" % path)

def lum_at(x, y):
        if y >= height or x >= width:
            return 255
        px = rows[y][x * channels:x * channels + 3]
        return lum(px)

    # The probe page keeps the ORIGINAL document's head styles, so a page with a
    # default body margin puts the canvas at (8, 8), not (0, 0). Locate the grid
    # by its alignment row instead of assuming an origin: the first line with a
    # long black run, then that run's left edge. Both are multiples of the 4px
    # cell, so the search is exact.
    y0 = -1
    x0 = -1
    for y in range(0, min(height, 64)):
        run = [x for x in range(0, min(width, 80))
               if lum_at(x, y) < 128]
        if len(run) >= 48:
            y0 = y
            x0 = run[0]
            break
    if y0 < 0:
        raise ValueError("%s: no alignment row found (is this a ffgeom probe shot?)"
                         % path)
    base = y0 & ~3

def bit(grid_row, cell, origin):
        return 1 if lum_at(origin + cell * 4 + 2, base + grid_row * 4 + 2) < 128 else 0

def probe(page, selector, out_html):
    import re
    with open(page) as f:
        src = f.read()
    # The page's own scripts must not run: the probe is how the harness measures
    # the no-JS document (javascript.enabled=false in the parity profile), but the
    # PROBE itself needs a script to run. Strip every existing <script> block, so
    # the only executable left is the probe's.
    src = re.sub(r"(?is)<script\b.*?</script>", "", src)
    script = PROBE_TMPL % selector
    with open(out_html, "w") as f:
        f.write(_append_probe(src, script))

def height_probe(page, out_html):
    import re
    with open(page) as f:
        src = f.read()
    src = re.sub(r"(?is)<script\b.*?</script>", "", src)
    # The height is carried on a synthetic #__ffh div appended at load, then read by
    # the SAME rect probe the geometry harness uses (a div's getBoundingClientRect
    # height is its CSS height here, so the canvas bit-grid machinery is reused and
    # trusted). The probe runs on load and replaces the body AFTER measuring.
    with open(out_html, "w") as f:
        f.write(_append_probe(src, HEIGHT_SCRIPT + PROBE_TMPL % "#__ffh"))

def height(path):
    """Decodes the scrollHeight carried by the #__ffh sentinel: the probe encodes
    one rect (its height), which decode() returns as the first element's h value."""
    vals = decode(path)
    if not vals:
        raise ValueError("%s: height probe produced no rect" % path)
    return vals[0][3]

guitime -- how long the REAL Freedom window takes from "navigate" to "painted and idle".  Not headless: the browser is the GUI binary running in a nested weston (Xvfb + weston, pixman renderer), loading the page through the same do_load/render/paint path a user's session takes. The only addition is FREEDOM_GUI_TIMING=<file>: once the page is loaded, no background job or JS tick is pending and no new frame was painted for 150 ms, the window writes {"ms": <last paint - navigation request>} and exits (FREEDOM_GUI_EXIT_AT_IDLE). Nothing is timed in a separate mode (spec/parity.md).  The page is measured under the corpus policy (FREEDOM_AS_HOST=corpus.test with tests/parity/hosts: presentation trust, JavaScript off), the same one `make parity` and tools/fftime.py use. A scratch profile directory keeps the user's own preferences out of the measurement. If Xvfb or weston is missing the tool says so and exits 2: it never falls back to a different, headless measurement.  Usage: guitime.py [--runs N] [--bin PATH] [--hosts DIR] <page.html> ... Prints one line per page:  <name>\t<median ms>\t<min>\t<max> Exit 0 when every page was measured, 1 on a failed measurement, 2 when the environment is missing.

def start_display(workdir):
    """Starts Xvfb and a nested weston; returns (env, processes) or None when unavailable."""
    for tool in ("Xvfb", "weston"):
        if shutil.which(tool) is None:
            print("guitime: %s not found: the GUI cannot be measured here" % tool, file=sys.stderr)
            return None
    num = 90 + os.getpid() % 9
    disp = ":%d" % num
    socket_name = "wl-guitime-%d" % os.getpid()
    runtime = os.environ.get("XDG_RUNTIME_DIR", "/run/user/%d" % os.getuid())
    xv = subprocess.Popen(["Xvfb", disp, "-screen", "0", "1600x1100x24"],
                          stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL, stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL)
    time.sleep(1.0)
    wenv = dict(os.environ, DISPLAY=disp)
    ws = subprocess.Popen(["weston", "--backend=x11-backend.so", "--renderer=pixman", "--width=1300",
                           "--height=900", "--socket=" + socket_name, "--no-config"],
                          env=wenv, stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL, stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL)
    sock = os.path.join(runtime, socket_name)
    for _ in range(START_ATTEMPTS):
        if os.path.exists(sock):
            break
        time.sleep(0.5)
    else:
        for p in (ws, xv):
            p.kill()
        print("guitime: weston did not come up", file=sys.stderr)
        return None
    env = dict(os.environ, WAYLAND_DISPLAY=socket_name, XDG_RUNTIME_DIR=runtime)
    return env, (ws, xv)

mutate -- compile-time mutation testing for the CMocka suites.  One mutant = one operator substitution in one src/ file that has a matching tests/test_<module>.c. The mutated source replaces the original for a single `make build/test_<module>` build and run, then the original is restored.  killed          the suite ran and at least one test failed survived        the suite passed on the mutated code (a blind spot) killed-by-build the mutation broke -Werror or the link (reported apart, because a syntax error is not the suite's work)  Exit status: 0 when every mutant died, 1 when any mutant survived.  The mutation set is deliberately mechanical (comparison/relational/logical/ arithmetic operators): each is one token swap on a line of the module's own code, never inside comments or strings. Only the first MUTATE_MAX sites per file are taken, in line order, so the run stays bounded.  Usage: tools/mutate.py [--max N] [--mods a,b,c] [--verbose]

pngprof -- structural ink-profile dump for page screenshots.  Build-time tool for Freedom layout work (companion to tools/pngdiff.c). Where pngdiff reduces two renders to one scalar score, pngprof prints WHERE the ink sits: the horizontal column profile split into vertical bands, and the cumulative vertical ink distribution. That is what turns a divergence like "slashdot col_mae 0.39" into a statement like "the article column spans x=120..600 in Firefox but x=0..950 in Freedom".  It answers the questions an agent cannot answer by looking at the PNG: with no image input available (or when the numbers matter more than the picture), the agent reads these profiles instead. Ink is defined against the image's modal background luminance, exactly like pngdiff, so a dark author theme and a forced light theme compare meaningfully.  Decoder: pure python (zlib + the five PNG filters), no third-party packages, so it runs anywhere the repo runs. RGBA/RGB/grey/16-bit screenshots all normalise to an 8-bit RGB row buffer. It reads only local files that the harness or the operator just produced; it never sees remote content and is not part of the browser's attack surface.  Usage: pngprof <image.png> [--bands N] [--cols C] [--rows R]  Output (stdout): - image width/height and the background luminance used - the column profile: C buckets, each printed as the ink fraction of that bucket's cells, repeated per vertical band

prune -- cut a corpus page down to ONE subtree, keeping its whole ancestor chain.  Isolating a layout bug on a 400 KB page by eye is slow; isolating it by deleting everything that is not on the path to the element is mechanical. The <head> (every <style> and <link>) is kept as is, so the cascade is untouched; in the <body> only the target subtree and its ancestors survive, with every other sibling dropped along the path. Scripts are removed (both engines render with JS off anyway).  Usage: prune.py <page.html> <xpath> <out.html> xpath  selects the element(s) to keep, e.g. '//nav[@class="nav-primary"]' Prints the number of matched elements; exits 1 when none matched.

        cs = r.headers.get_content_charset() or "utf-8"
